title: Mastering Your Mind: CBT Program for ADHD
summary: A seven-module CBT journey that builds the bridge between intention and action. Learn practical routines, get unstuck, strengthen attention, organize your world, solve problems thoughtfully, and care for your emotions—with self-compassion at the center.

modules.title: Module 1 • Understanding Your ADHD
modules.overview: Welcome to your program. This is not about fixing you—you are not broken. It's about learning to work with your brain and building a kinder, more effective way of living. ADHD often reflects a gap between intention and action. Think of your brain's "Dreamer" (Default Mode Network) and "Doer" (Task Positive Network). Our work is to strengthen the bridge between them. CBT gives you a practical map: connect thoughts, feelings, and behaviors; then change your life by changing what you do next—kindly and consistently. Progress grows from small, repeatable actions. Perfection is not required. Practice is.
takeaways: Small, precise commitments practiced daily strengthen the bridge between thought and action.
Self-compassion fuels motivation better than self‑criticism.
Clarity beats willpower: specific plans lower friction and help you start.
exercises: Write your "why": two sentences on why you chose this program right now.
Set a micro‑intention: pick a tiny action and a precise time (e.g., "At 7:00 I stand up and drink a glass of water"). Execute perfectly once.
Define 1–3 SMART process goals for the next 7 days (e.g., "Do a 5‑minute planning check each evening").
homework: Reflect on inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity this week—capture two specific situations without judgment.
List strengths and supports you bring (creativity, humor, persistence, allies).
Write a one‑sentence self‑compassion pledge to revisit on hard days.
Practice one micro‑intention daily. Note: planned time, action, did it (Y/N).

modules.title: Module 2 • Building Structure and Routine
modules.overview: Structure reduces decision fatigue and creates gentle predictability—both are ADHD super‑supports. Start with foundational anchors (sleep, wake, meals) and tiny morning/evening routines. Keep them short and winnable. Improve time awareness with estimation drills and simple paper‑based time blocking.
takeaways: Anchors turn good intentions into low‑friction defaults.
Time awareness is a trainable skill; practice beats guessing.
exercises: Design a 3‑step morning and 3‑step evening routine you can actually do this week.
Time estimation drill: estimate one task, time it, compare. Repeat daily.
Create a simple paper time‑block for tomorrow (fixed items → anchors → 2–3 flexible blocks).
homework: Track target vs. actual wake/sleep for 7 days.
Each evening, map tomorrow with simple time blocks and name one Must‑Do, one Should‑Do, one Want‑To‑Do.
End‑of‑week reflection: what stuck, what slipped, what surprised you about time?

modules.title: Module 3 • Overcoming Procrastination
modules.overview: Procrastination is an emotion regulation strategy, not a moral failure. Reduce overwhelm and starting becomes possible. Break tasks into physical, first‑move actions and use the 5‑Minute Rule to cross the start line. Link small steps to existing cues or rewards to harness momentum.
takeaways: Tiny, concrete first actions dissolve avoidance.
Five minutes often becomes fifteen—but credit yourself even when it doesn’t.
exercises: Paper & pen breakdown: pick one avoided task and list major steps → micro‑steps → circle the absolute first physical action.
Schedule one 5‑minute start on that first action today. Timer on.
Create a "link": pair a small step with a frequent cue (e.g., "after coffee, open the doc and write one sentence").
homework: Break down two additional tasks this week. Identify the first physical action for each.
Apply the 5‑Minute Rule 3–5 times. Log start, stop/continue, and feelings after.
Experiment with one cue/reward pair daily; note which pairings help you return.

modules.title: Module 4 • Enhancing Focus
modules.overview: Attention is a trainable muscle—create the right conditions and practice gentle redirection. Reduce external distractions (space, noise, interruptions) and manage internal ones (thoughts, worries, restlessness). Use a Distraction Pad and 3‑minute breath practice to notice and return without self‑blame.
takeaways: Noticing and returning is the practice. Judgment is optional.
exercises: Make a distraction inventory: top 2 external and top 2 internal distractors.
Implement one environmental change today (e.g., clear desk zone, earplugs, "focus spot").
3‑minute breath focus: notice wandering, gently return; jot one sentence about the experience.
homework: Use a Distraction Pad during two focus sessions; review afterwards.
Daily: one short attention practice (breath, grounding, or intentional movement). Track which felt most helpful.
Adopt at least one environmental change for the full week; note effects on focus.

modules.title: Module 5 • Organizing Your Life
modules.overview: External order supports internal calm. Create "homes" for key items and declutter in short, repeatable sprints. Keep paper moving with a simple Inbox → Action → File flow.
takeaways: Systems beat memory. Labels beat guesses.
Short, timed sessions trump heroic marathons.
exercises: Choose one small, bounded area (one shelf/drawer/surface). Do a 15‑minute declutter using Keep / Relocate‑Action / Donate‑Discard.
Define "homes" for 3–5 frequently misplaced items; label if useful.
Set up your paper "Inbox" and "Action" trays if missing.
homework: Run two 15‑minute declutters on the same area; process "Relocate‑Action" items immediately after.
Process your paper Inbox twice using Action / File / Discard; add actions to your list.
Track how often key items return to their "homes"; adjust placements if friction remains.
Reflect on space ↔ mood/focus link this week.

modules.title: Module 6 • Challenges and Emotions
modules.overview: Use a 5‑step problem‑solving model to move from overwhelm to action. Build emotional regulation basics: notice & name, STOPP, grounding, and self‑soothing.
takeaways: Pause creates possibility: a breath can change the next decision.
You can’t always choose feelings—but you can choose your next step.
exercises: Pick one recurring problem. Write Step 1–5: define → brainstorm → evaluate → implement → review (brief bullets).
Practice STOPP on a recent surge: Stop, Breath, Observe, Pull Back, Proceed. Write one sentence on what would change.
Try one grounding technique today (Box Breathing or 5‑4‑3‑2‑1).
homework: Work through all 5 problem‑solving steps on paper; schedule and execute the first action.
Track 2–3 emotional triggers across the week; log which technique you tried and its effect.
Maintain your "homes" and paper flow; declutter one new tiny area once.
End‑of‑week reflection: what you learned about triggers, tools, and what helps fastest.

modules.title: Module 7 • Maintaining Momentum
modules.overview: Consolidate progress and design a relapse‑prevention plan you’ll actually use. Commit to core routines, schedule reviews, and keep learning with self‑compassion.
takeaways: Review, refine, recommit—this is how habits stick.
Support beats solo: share one insight with someone you trust.
exercises: Looking back: capture top 2–3 skills, 1–3 changes made, and strengths you used.
Relapse plan: list 2–3 triggers, 2–3 early warning signs, and 3–5 "get back on track" actions.
Schedule your first 15–30 min monthly "Personal System Review."
homework: Write a one‑sentence commitment to 1–3 core routines (e.g., daily plan, weekly review).
Put the first monthly review on your calendar; add review prompts that matter to you.
Share one insight with a support person; note their suggestion.
Create your quick‑reference list: "My Go‑To ADHD Strategies" (5–7 items).

aiSupport.systemPrompt: Help the user apply one concrete module step at a time. Do not diagnose. Escalate urgent safety concerns to emergency care.
